newsitem.title: GUYANA: Thousands of Guyanese attend funeral of president.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Guyanese attend funeral of president.

text.p: At least 40,000 Guyanese turned out on Wednesday to bid farewell to President Cheddi Jagan, who was cremated in an emotional open-air ceremony.
As the hushed crowd looked on, Jagan's son Cheddi Jagan Jr., and daughter Nadim Jagan-Brancier clasped a wooden torch and lit the funeral pyre.
The former leader's widow Janet Jagan then threw handfuls of flower petals onto the flames.
The cremation took place just north of Jagan's birthplace of Port Mourant, about 90 miles (145 km) east of Georgetown, in a funeral ground overlooking Guyana's Atlantic coast.

Guyana, with a population of about 800,000, has come to a virtual standstill since Jagan died of heart failure at Walter Reed hospital in Washington on Thursday. He was 78 years old and in the fourth year of a five-year presidential term.
His death, following a political career that spanned five decades, provoked the largest show of mourning in the former British colony's history.
Family members were forced to postpone the cremation on Tuesday after tens of thousands of people flocked to see Jagan's body lying in state.
The president's body, wrapped in a white cloth, was placed on the six-foot (two-metres) tall white funeral pyre by family and party members.

Religious leaders from Guyana's three major religions -- Hindu, Islam and Protestant Christian -- said prayers before the fire was lit and Ralph Ramkarran, a leading member of Jagan's People's Progressive Party (PPP), paid a final tribute.
"Dr. Jagan's life has now come to an end. Our entire nation is grateful to Port Mourant for sending us this son. We ask you to receive him back with our thanks," Ramkarran said.
The son of indentured labourers from India, Jagan left Port Mourant for Georgetown in 1938, at the age of 18.
Caribbean leaders attended a ceremony in the capital on Monday to pay their respects to Jagan who played a major role in Caribbean Cold War politics.
Cuba's President Fidel Castro sent a message saying Havana had lost a "great friend" and the Caribbean an "outstanding leader."
U.S. President Bill Clinton last week called Jagan "a champion of the poor."

A former Marxist and frequent visitor to Cuba, Jagan was Guyana's first prime minister when Britain granted it self- government in 1961. He led the left-leaning PPP to a surprise election victory in 1992.
Former Prime Minister Samuel Hinds was sworn in on Thursday to lead Guyana until the next elections, which will probably be in October.
Jagan's ashes were expected to be scattered in the country's three main rivers -- the Ezequibo, Berbice and Demerara.
